🇺🇸 Katie Zacharia steps into the spotlight with a short first briefing as Trump's press secretary

In a tightly managed 14-minute debut at the White House podium on October 13, new press secretary Katie Zacharia highlighted the administration's priorities, confirmed a request for the resignation of Ambassador Kimberly Guilfoyle, and drew a positive reaction from President Donald Trump even as the session ended abruptly.

Zacharia, a California-based conservative commentator and mother of four who previously advised Trump Media and Technology Group, assumed the role after Karoline Leavitt departed in August following the birth of her second child. Trump announced the appointment on October 9, describing Zacharia as a loyal supporter with an unblemished record of backing his agenda from the start. She had held a brief position at the Department of Homeland Security earlier in the year before returning to private-sector communications work.

At the lectern in the James S. Brady Press Briefing Room, Zacharia opened by expressing gratitude for the opportunity and noting her longstanding desire to serve in the administration. She pointed to ongoing campaign activity ahead of the midterms, emphasizing themes of economic gains, border security, and the president's personal engagement with voters. The session moved quickly to questions from just three outlets—Breitbart News, Fox News, and the Daily Mail—before she concluded by directing further inquiries to Trump as he prepared to depart for a campaign stop in Alaska.

The most substantive development came when Zacharia stated that the administration had asked Guilfoyle, the U.S. ambassador to Greece and a former Fox News personality, to resign amid reports of improper conduct. She described Guilfoyle as a valued contributor and wished her well, offering no further details during the brief exchange. Guilfoyle later indicated she would step down while rejecting the underlying claims.

A momentary verbal slip occurred when Zacharia, discussing family considerations and the demands of the job, referred to her husband as "my president" before correcting herself. The remark drew attention in coverage of the event, alongside observations about her delivery and the limited scope of the Q&A. Trump, speaking to reporters as he walked to Marine One, said he thought she had done very well and offered an approving assessment of the appearance.

The choice of Zacharia continues a pattern of elevating figures with strong public alignment to the administration's messaging, particularly those experienced in conservative media. With midterm elections approaching, the press secretary's role centers on projecting consistency around policy outcomes in areas such as employment, energy production, and prescription drug costs—points Zacharia referenced in her opening remarks. Her short first outing leaves open questions about how the briefing room will function under her tenure, but the president's immediate public endorsement signals internal support for the selection.

Shanghai ATP Masters 1000 R16 

Casper Ruud vs Felix Auger-Aliassime

14 October 2026 | 12:30 Shanghai time | Outdoor hard

🧠 Form & Context

Casper Ruud

📊 Ruud’s CFS is 53.7, trailing Auger-Aliassime by 8.9 points. His filtered last ten overall and hard-court records are 5–5, with a 35–19 overall record over 52 weeks.
🎾 He has two straight-set wins here, over Yunchaokete 6–1, 7–6(2) and Tien 6–4, 7–6(3). They follow a straight-set defeat to Darderi in Tokyo.
🛡️ His serve offers a credible route to a close match: 89.2% holds, 56.4% second-serve points won and 71.8% break points saved.
⚠️ The recent hard-court sample is spread out: his last-ten hard sequence reaches back to February. His Cincinnati match ended in retirement in August, and his tiebreak win rate is 47.1%.

Felix Auger-Aliassime

📈 Auger-Aliassime leads the CFS at 62.6. His filtered last ten overall and hard-court records are 6–4, with a 50–21 overall record over 52 weeks.
🔄 Both Shanghai victories needed three sets: 4–6, 7–6(1), 7–5 against Ugo Carabelli, then 6–3, 4–6, 6–1 against Carreno Busta. He has advanced through completed matches, but neither was a clean two-set performance.
🎯 His ATP hard record over 52 weeks is 33–13, against Ruud’s 16–12. He wins 78.8% of first-serve points and holds 88.3% of service games.
🧱 His 75.9% tiebreak win rate is a significant advantage in a matchup between strong servers. The limitation is his 17.2% return-games win rate, which leaves Ruud room to protect serve.

🔍 Match Breakdown

Both players have strong service numbers and modest return-games win rates. Ruud can keep sets close by landing first serves and relying on his second ball against a returner who breaks relatively infrequently. Auger-Aliassime’s broader ATP hard record gives him the stronger surface case.

If sets reach a tiebreak, the historical comparison favours Auger-Aliassime by 28.8 percentage points. That does not decide an individual tiebreak, but it weakens the idea that Ruud’s serve alone is enough to justify backing him to take a set.

Their latest meeting, Monte Carlo in April, ended with Ruud retiring at 5–7, 2–2. It cannot support a normal match-performance conclusion. The latest completed hard meeting listed was Cincinnati 2024, where Auger-Aliassime prevailed 6–3, 6–1; it is relevant context, but old enough to carry limited weight. His two dropped sets this week keep us from promoting the favourite to an active position.

text:
Black parents walked their own children to the front of the line, three weeks after a massacre. That was Fifth Avenue on July 28, 1917, when several hundred children dressed head to foot in white stepped off behind muffled drums with thousands of grown folks falling in behind them. Twenty thousand people packed both sidewalks and watched them go by without hearing one word for thirty-four blocks.

The sign was a drawing, blown up large and mounted on a pole so a person could hold it above their head. It showed a Black woman down on her knees in front of the President of the United States.

She was asking him to bring democracy home to America before he shipped it across the ocean to Europe. A police officer looked at that picture on Fifth Avenue on the morning of Saturday, July 28, 1917, and ruled it out of the parade.

The organizers pulled it from the line. Thousands of Black New Yorkers were about to walk thirty-four blocks down the richest street in America without saying one word out loud.

And a drawing was still too much.

To understand why anybody would draw a woman on her knees, you have to go west, to a river town in Illinois where the packing plants had been hiring.

Mabel Randall was twenty-four years old and had been living in East St. Louis about a year and a half. On the evening of July 2, 1917, the windows and the door of her house came in.

She got down under the bed with her child and stayed there until dark. When it was dark enough to move, she went next door and asked the white woman who lived there if they could hide underneath her house.

The woman said no. She said she had chickens in the yard.

So Mabel Randall found a coal house instead, and she and her people piled stoves on top of themselves and lay there until four in the morning. Then she walked to the railroad yards, waited an hour and a half, and made the ferry across the river to St. Louis with what she had on her back.

That is the East St. Louis massacre in one household.

Now multiply it by six thousand people put out of their homes in roughly a day.

The reason was money, and nobody bothered hiding it. White workers at the packing houses and the aluminum plant had walked out on strike, and the companies filled the empty jobs with Black workers coming up from the South.

In late May, six hundred union men marched on City Hall to demand the city stop the new arrivals. The secretary of the Central Trades and Labor Union put the grievance in writing, complaining that ten thousand undesirable Negroes had poured in and suggesting something be done to get rid of a portion of the ones already there.

Five weeks later the town came apart.

Mineola McGee was a chambermaid. She earned three dollars and fifty cents a week and had been in East St. Louis since the eighth of February.

On Tuesday morning, sometime between seven and eight o'clock, she walked to her job at Mrs. Gray's house and reached for the door. The bullet caught her in the arm.

She said afterward that the only two people she could see anywhere on that street were a soldier and a policeman, and that she believed it was one of those two who shot her. She fainted, and came to in the back of a patrol wagon.

At the hospital they took the rest of the arm off. When she gave her statement to the investigators, she added two more things at the end of it.

She had not been able to find one relative since it happened, not the cousins, not the aunt, not the uncle.

And no insurance.

Narcis Gurley was seventy-one years old. She had lived in that city for thirty years, keeping roomers and taking in laundry, which is thirty years of somebody else's shirts.

She watched the house near hers catch, and she heard men out in the street, so she stayed inside, because the street was worse than the room. Then her own roof started coming down on her.

She came out badly burned. A white man in the crowd said to leave the old women alone, and that one sentence from a stranger is the only reason she lived.

She lost everything she had.

Rena Cook had been out fishing that day. She was riding home on the Alton streetcar with her husband and her son when a crowd stopped the car at Collinsville and Broadway and ordered the white passengers off.

Then they came in and took her husband and her boy. Both of them were killed in the street, and two policemen stood there and watched it happen.

She was beaten until she lost consciousness, and woke up two days later in St. Mary's Hospital.

Lulu Robinson was thirty-three and eight months into her new life in that city. Between five and six on Monday evening the shots started coming through her walls, and she and her twelve-year-old son backed up against the plaster trying to get out of the way of them.

She was hit three times, in a finger, in the shoulder, in the face. Her son was hit twice and died.

She never saw her husband again.

The official count of Black dead in East St. Louis was thirty-nine. The NAACP sent W. E. B. Du Bois and the writer Martha Gruening out there to take statements and photographs in person, and what they published in The Crisis that September put the real number somewhere between one and two hundred.

Around four hundred thousand dollars in property burned, Black-owned and white-owned both. Nine white residents also died.

A reporter for the St. Louis Star watched an elderly woman walk past the police station that night carrying everything she had left in the world. It came to a worn pair of shoes, which she was not wearing because she was barefoot, one extra calico dress, an old shawl, and two puppies.

She was crying, and she went by the lit windows of City Hall without seeing anybody, because there was nowhere in particular for her to go.

Days later, Martha Gruening found another woman poking through the ashes of her own house. She was sixty-five, her family had gotten out, and almost nothing else had.

She asked Gruening a question this country has still not answered properly.

We can't live South and they don't want us North. Where are we to go?

Then came the part that turned the grief into something harder.

Near Cahokia Creek, Gruening fell into conversation with two young Illinois militiamen from a town called Olney. They boasted to her about what had been done to people in that water.

She asked them how many they had killed themselves. They were vague about the count, but they were perfectly clear that they had been shooting to kill.

She took it to the Military Board of Inquiry and offered to travel anywhere, Olney included, to point the two of them out. The board asked her whether she supposed the boys had only been showing off for a lady.

They said such jesting was in bad taste, but boys will be boys. They told her identification was impossible now, because those troops had already been sent home, and that it was rather late in the proceedings to be raising it at all.

Then seven officers in a room gave a woman a lecture about her heavy responsibility as a writer, and warned her not to leave the world with the wrong impression of the Illinois militia. They said they had gone through the evidence exhaustively and found not one instance of misconduct.

Gruening asked them one question back. If there had been that much heroism, how did so many Black people end up dead and only eight white men?

There was no answer to that.

That was what New York was reading in July of 1917. Not rumor, and not a number.

Names, ages, weekly wages, street addresses, and a file already being closed.

James Weldon Johnson called a meeting at St. Philip's Church in Harlem. He had been the NAACP's field secretary for barely a year.

The room floated the sensible plan, which was to rent Carnegie Hall and hold a protest meeting indoors, the way respectable organizations expressed themselves. Johnson wanted Fifth Avenue.

He remembered a suggestion made at an NAACP conference the year before, by Oswald Garrison Villard, about what a crowd could do by marching and making no sound at all. Villard's own mother had led a silent peace parade in 1914, and Johnson took the whole shape of it, the mourning clothes and the covered drums, and turned it on lynching.

They had ten days to build it.

Pastors were asked to empty their pews into the street. A leaflet went out dated July 24 with a section printed on it under the heading "Why We March."

It said they marched to make another Waco, another Memphis, another East St. Louis impossible, and to see the people responsible answer for it. It said they marched because they considered it a crime to stay quiet in the face of such acts.

It said they marched because they wanted their children to live in a better land than the one that had fallen to them. At the bottom it asked people to be in line on Saturday and show they had not gone numb to the sorrows of their own race.

The Reverend Charles Martin, a West Indian minister who founded the Fourth Moravian Church, put his name to it. He signed off yours in righteous indignation.

Saturday arrived in the middle of a record heat wave. They gathered on Fifth Avenue between 55th and 59th in the kind of July air that glues a collar to a neck, and the men were dressed in wool.

The children went to the front. Several hundred of them, dressed head to foot in white.

Sit with what that decision actually was. Three weeks after a mob had gone through a neighborhood in Illinois and not spared the children in it, several hundred Black parents in New York walked their own children to the head of a line and sent them out ahead of everybody.

Behind the children came the women, thousands of them, also in white. The men were last, in dark suits, and some of them wore United States Army uniforms, because Black soldiers had already landed in France that spring.

At the very front walked the drummers. The drums were muffled, wrapped so the sound came out low, and they kept a slow cadence, the beat you hear at a funeral instead of a parade.

Then the first drumbeat landed and the whole street started moving. Nobody chanted, and nobody sang.

Crossing 50th they went by St. Patrick's Cathedral, and at 42nd they went by the library. Through the thirties they passed department stores where they were welcome to spend money and not welcome to stand behind the counter.

Mounted police rode the flanks the entire way. Around twenty thousand people packed both sidewalks to watch, Black and white together, and plenty of the white ones had no idea what they were looking at.

So Black Boy Scouts moved through the crowd handing out the leaflet, because the marchers had agreed not to explain themselves out loud. The explaining was left to the banners, and they came down the avenue one behind another like sentences in a letter.

One counted 2,867 Black Americans lynched in thirty-one years and pointed out that not one murderer had suffered for any of it. One said race prejudice is the offspring of ignorance and the mother of lynching.

One asked mothers whether lynchers go to heaven. One said, with no decoration at all, that their hands were full of blood.

One reminded Fifth Avenue that the first blood spilled for American independence belonged to a Black man named Crispus Attucks. One did plain arithmetic, that they had fought for the liberty of white Americans in six wars, and their reward was East St. Louis.

And one, up near the head of the line, put the question to the President that the country was working very hard not to hear. Mr. President, why not make America safe for democracy?

Somewhere in that procession was a gap where a drawing should have been.

James Weldon Johnson wrote later that the streets of New York had witnessed a great many strange sights, and he judged they had never witnessed one stranger than this. He also noticed that some of the people standing on the curb were crying.

The line held the whole way. Past the hotels, past the churches, past the shops, thirty-four blocks of people refusing to make a sound while a city stared at them and their children walked out front.

At 23rd Street, at Madison Square, they finally broke ranks. And a few cheers got loose.

That was the first noise out of them since 57th Street.

Four days later, on the first of August, eleven of them were standing inside the White House with a scheduled appointment. They had brought a petition with them.

The names on it included James Weldon Johnson, the Harlem realtor John E. Nail, the Reverend Frederick A. Cullen, and the clubwoman Maria C. Lawton. Madam C. J. Walker was there too, a woman who had come up out of the Louisiana cotton fields and built a fortune selling hair products to Black women.

Their paper reminded the President that Black men were wearing his country's uniform in France at that exact hour. It asked him to make lynching a federal crime.

Joseph Tumulty, the President's secretary, came out and told them Wilson was too busy to receive them. They had traveled down from New York for an appointment arranged in advance, and now they stood in a corridor while a man explained the President's schedule to them.

They left the petition on a desk and went home.

Two weeks later Wilson sat with a smaller group and heard them out. Eleven months after that, in July of 1918, he issued a written statement discouraging mob violence.

It went out to the press, he never spoke it aloud, and it never asked Congress for a law.

The killing did not slow down.

The number of lynchings in America rose after the parade and did not fall back below the 1917 level until 1923. The Dyer Anti-Lynching Bill was introduced the next year and died.

Something close to two hundred anti-lynching bills were put before Congress between the end of the Civil War and the civil rights movement, and every last one of them was killed, most in the Senate. Lynching became a federal crime on March 29, 2022.

One hundred and five years after those people walked down Fifth Avenue without saying a word to ask for exactly that.

Two sets of photographers worked the route that Saturday, the Underwood and Underwood studio and a man named Cyril T. Adams. Their prints sit at Yale today, inside the papers James Weldon Johnson and his wife Grace kept for the rest of their lives.

You can look at the children in white any time you want. What you cannot look at is the sign that got pulled.

No photograph of it exists in the parade record, because it never entered the parade. All that survives of it is a sentence in the next morning's New York Times, describing what it had shown.

So the only place left in this country where that woman is still on her knees in front of that President is inside a description, in an old newspaper, in a paragraph almost nobody reads.

A description weighs nothing at all. It costs about ten seconds to hand to somebody else.

Picture it one time before you go. A drawing on a pole, walked back down the sidewalk at 57th Street and out of the line, past thousands of people who had already agreed not to say a word.

LCI INDUSTRIES $LCII YIELDS 5.8% ONLY UNTIL ITS MERGER CLOSES. THE JUSTICE DEPARTMENT JUST ASKED FOR A CLOSER LOOK AT THAT MERGER:

The Income Len5 is watching LCI Industries (LCII) at $79.34, +$0.20 / +0.25% on Tuesday.

The Elkhart, Indiana company sells under the Lippert name and makes the axles, chassis, slide-out rooms and windows built into RVs. In June it agreed to be bought, in an all-stock deal, by Patrick Industries (PATK) at $64.34, +$0.14 / +0.22% on Tuesday. Just after 4:30pm ET Tuesday, after the close, both companies said the U.S. Department of Justice wants more information before the deal can go ahead.

The verdict: LCI's dividend is real and well covered, and it has an end date. At closing, each LCI share becomes 1.2440 Patrick shares, and at Patrick's current dividend those pay about half of today's check. Tuesday's news pushes that end date later and makes it less certain.

The two checks, per LCI share:

- LCI today: $1.15 a quarter, 5.8% a year at Tuesday's close.
- 1.2440 Patrick shares at its current $0.47: about $0.58 a quarter, 2.9% a year at the same price (arithmetic).

The combined company has not set its dividend; the deal announcement promised buybacks and "a balanced dividend policy."

Until closing, the merger agreement lets LCI keep paying up to $1.15, and the cash is there. Free cash flow, the cash left after running the business and paying for equipment, was about $287M in the 12 months to June 30 (arithmetic). The dividend costs about $112M a year. That cash covers it about 2.6 times.

The review clock:

- October 9: as its 30-day review was due to end, the Justice Department sent what lawyers call a second request, a demand for more documents and data.
- The deal cannot close until 30 days after both companies substantially answer it. They have agreed to work to answer within six months at most.
- Contract deadline: March 30, 2027, extending automatically to as late as September 30, 2027, if only regulatory approval is missing.
- If regulators demand it, the companies must accept selling businesses that bring in up to roughly 7% of their combined 2025 sales. Beyond that, neither has to.

For an income holder, the delay cuts both ways. Each extra quarter the deal stays open can mean another full $1.15 instead of about $0.58. It is also more time for the Justice Department to demand bigger sales of businesses, or to sue to block the deal.

Since June, LCI's price has mostly been Patrick's price:

- Deal value on June 29, the last close before the announcement: $115.92 per LCI share, 15.8% above LCI's $100.12.
- Deal value at Tuesday's close: $80.04, 31% less (arithmetic).

The offer was in shares, not dollars, so it fell with Patrick. LCI trades 0.9% under it, and both stocks hit one-year lows on Monday.

Patrick, also based in Elkhart, makes parts for RVs, boats and homes. Its RV sales fell 15% in the June quarter. It carries $1.42B of debt against $1.13B of owners' equity. In the June quarter alone it handed owners $106M, mostly in buybacks. That is the company whose dividend policy LCI holders would inherit. Patrick is on none of the six Len5 watchlists, and debt above its owners' stake keeps it off the Quality Len5 too.

The six Len5es on LCI:

- Income: STRONG on the check, with an expiry date, #2 of 30. It hunts cash paid to owners that a business can keep paying. LCI pays out 53% of its past year's profit, and free cash covers the dividend 2.6 times. The weak half is time. What would knock LCI off the Income Len5: the merger closing, when its shares stop trading.

- Momentum: NOT A FIT. It hunts stocks climbing for months on company news; LCI closed 50% under its February 12 high of $159.66. What would put LCI on the Momentum Len5: months of gains in Patrick's shares, which LCI now follows.

- Quality-Value: NOT A FIT, a cautious read. It hunts a durable business at a discount. About 9 times the past year's profit looks like a discount; durability is the doubt. RV shipments are down 14.2% this year through August, per the RV Industry Association. What would put LCI on the Quality-Value Len5: shipments holding steady for several quarters with the price still near 9 times profit.

- Deep-Value & Special-Situations: NOT A FIT, tentative. It hunts a sound business priced below a cautious value, or a dated event that changes the math. The merger sets LCI's price by formula, so the price measures Patrick, not LCI. What would put LCI on the Deep-Value & Special-Situations Len5: the deal falling apart, leaving LCI priced on its own.

- Growth: NOT A FIT, tentative. It hunts years of rising profit at a fair price. June-quarter profit rose to $2.75 a share from $2.29 on cost cuts and tariff refunds, while sales fell 12.5%. What would put LCI on the Growth Len5: sales growing again, not just margins.

- Hypergrowth: NOT A FIT. It hunts very fast sales growth; LCI forecasts $3.9B-$4.1B of 2026 sales, about where the past 12 months landed. What would put LCI on the Hypergrowth Len5: sales growth in the tens of percent.

LCI also fits the Quality Len5, a profitable, sound business at any price: past-year profit of $211.3M is about 15% of owners' equity (arithmetic), and its $852.6M of debt sits well under that $1.43B stake.

What comes next:

- Wednesday: the first session to trade on the news.
- Third-quarter results: no date set; last year's came October 30.
- Mid-November: last year's December dividend was declared November 13. Another $1.15 would show the review has not touched the check.

The bigger risk to the check is the RV slump, not the review: if shipments keep falling, the cash covering $1.15 shrinks, deal or no deal.

Tuesday's news did not touch the check. It moved the expiry, and for now nobody has put a new date on it.
